members.prompt:
You have watched a three-round debate on:

> A team of AI agents does better work than a single AI model

Decide which side argued better — judge argument quality and logical
clarity, not your own opinion of the topic. Announce the winner and
explain your decision in one paragraph.

content: **Opening argument:** The core advantage of a team of AI agents is that errors get caught. A single model working alone has one pass, one perspective, and a known tendency to commit early to a line of reasoning and rationalize it. A team can split the work into roles: one agent drafts, another critiques, a third checks facts or runs tests. That turns blind spots into points of friction where mistakes surface. The evidence supports this. Multi-agent debate setups (e.g., Du et al., 2023) improved factual accuracy and math reasoning over the same model answering alone. Simpler ensemble methods like self-consistency, which sample several reasoning paths and take the majority answer, reliably beat single-pass answers on reasoning benchmarks. In software engineering, systems that pair a "coder" agent with a "tester" or "reviewer" agent catch bugs a lone generator ships. Teams also let you specialize and parallelize: separate agents can research, plan, and verify at the same time, each with a focused context window, instead of one model juggling everything at once. This mirrors why human institutions use peer review, editors, and second opinions. Raw intelligence isn't enough; checks and diverse perspectives are what turn good work into reliable work. To be fair, teams cost more compute and can fail when poorly coordinated. But when the question is which produces *better work*, structured collaboration has the edge.

**Rebuttal:** My opponent's evidence proves less than it seems. Self-consistency isn't a team at all. It's one model sampled several times and majority-voted, so it supports "more compute helps," not "multiple agents help." That confound runs through the debate literature too. When researchers give a single model a matched compute budget and strong prompting, much of the multi-agent advantage shrinks or disappears (e.g., Wang et al., 2024, "Rethinking the Bounds of LLM Reasoning"). The peer-review analogy also breaks down. Human reviewers bring different training, knowledge, and incentives. Copies of the same model share the same blind spots, so "critique" often means one instance confidently ratifying another's error. Debate agents are known to converge on a confident wrong answer rather than surface the right one.

**My argument:** Teams introduce a new failure mode that single models don't have: coordination loss. Every handoff between agents compresses context. The critic doesn't see everything the drafter considered. The tester doesn't know the design intent. The subagents make implicit decisions that conflict with each other. Empirical studies of multi-agent systems (e.g., Cemri et al., 2025, "Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?") find that many failures come from exactly this: misaligned roles, lost information between agents, and premature or skipped verification, not from weak individual models. That's why some practitioners building real agentic products have publicly argued for a single agent with full, continuous context over fragmented teams. Better work usually comes from coherence: one mind holding the whole problem. Adding agents mostly adds seams where that coherence can tear.

**Rebuttal and new argument:** My opponent is right that self-consistency is one model sampled repeatedly and that compute is a real confound. But coordination loss is not an argument against teams. It is a list of engineering bugs. Cemri et al. catalog *fixable* failures (unclear roles, dropped information, skipped verification), and they show that better role specification and verification protocols improve results. The "one mind holding the whole problem" alternative has its own seams. Single models degrade over long contexts, losing track of information buried in the middle and drifting from earlier constraints. Moving the work to one context window doesn't remove the problem. It hides it.

My strongest remaining point answers the "shared blind spots" objection directly: good teams are *heterogeneous* and *grounded*. You don't have to staff a team with clones. Mixture-of-Agents (Wang et al., 2024) combined different open models and outscored GPT-4o on AlpacaEval 2.0, which no single member could do alone. And a verifier agent doesn't have to just "agree." It can run the code, execute the tests, or query a source, so its critique rests on external evidence rather than the drafter's reasoning. This exploits a real asymmetry: checking an answer is usually easier than producing one. A team built to use that asymmetry, with different models and tools that touch reality, catches errors that a single model, however coherent, will confidently carry to the end.

**Rebuttal:** My opponent's strongest point actually supports my side. A verifier that runs code, executes tests, or queries a source is powerful because of the *tool*, not the *teammate*. A single agent can run the same tests and check the same sources itself, with full knowledge of why it wrote the code the way it did. That is the compute confound again, in a new form: grounding helps, but grounding is not teamwork.

The verification asymmetry is also narrower than claimed. Checking is cheap when a cheap checker exists, such as unit tests or a math answer. For essays, strategy, or design there is no oracle, and a critic agent is just another opinion with less context.

Mixture-of-Agents is a fair example of heterogeneity. But AlpacaEval is a preference benchmark judged by an LLM, MoA spent several times the inference of its single-model baseline, and the edge came from pooling *different* strong models. A comparably resourced single frontier model is the right comparison, and such models have since overtaken those scores.

"Fixable engineering bugs" concedes my point for now. The usual fix is giving agents more shared context, which moves the system back toward one mind. Long-context degradation is real, but splitting the work doesn't cure it. Someone still has to integrate the pieces, and that integrator works with *less* information, not more.

**My argument:** The strongest trend cuts against teams. The draft-critique-revise loop that multi-agent systems build externally is being learned *inside* single models. Reasoning models are trained to generate, check, backtrack, and verify within one continuous chain of thought, with no handoffs and nothing lost between roles. As this happens, the reported gains from bolting on debate or critic agents tend to shrink. The team structure was a scaffold that compensated for models that couldn't yet check themselves. When you compare fairly, with the same tools, the same compute, and a capable model, a single agent typically matches or beats the team. It is also cheaper, easier to debug, and produces a more coherent final product. "Better work" should mean better under equal conditions, and under equal conditions the team advantage mostly reflects extra resources rather than collaboration.

**Rebuttal:** My opponent says reasoning models now draft, check, and backtrack inside one chain of thought. But that internal check runs on the same weights, the same context, and the same assumptions that produced the error. Huang et al. (2023, "Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet") found that intrinsic self-correction without outside feedback often fails to help and sometimes makes answers worse. So "full knowledge of why it wrote the code that way" is exactly the problem. The author's rationale is what blinds it. A verifier with a *fresh* context doesn't inherit those assumptions, and that independence is a property of the teammate, not the tool. Better reasoning models don't make teams obsolete either. They make better teammates.

**My argument:** The "equal compute" framing assumes that a single agent could use a team's budget equally well. Often it can't. A single agent works serially within one context window, so beyond some point extra compute just means a longer, more degraded trace. Teams are how you turn more compute into better work on large problems: broad research, big codebases, many-source analysis. Anthropic reported that its multi-agent research system, a lead agent directing parallel subagents, outperformed a single Claude Opus 4 agent by about 90% on its internal research evaluation. To be honest, Anthropic also found that token usage explained much of that gain, and it noted that multi-agent setups suit some tasks (like tightly coupled coding) less well. That caveat makes my point rather than weakening it. On problems too broad for one context, the team structure is what lets the extra compute pay off. For the work that matters most, "better" is not a lab tie under artificial budget limits. It is what you can accomplish when the task outgrows one mind, and that is where teams win.

**Rebuttal:** Huang et al. actually cuts against my opponent. The same paper tested multi-agent debate and found it did no better than self-consistency with an equal number of responses. What failed was correction *without external feedback*, and a second instance of the same model is not external feedback. A fresh context resets the assumptions in the window, not the weights, so the critic shares the author's training-level blind spots. When outside signal does help, it comes from tests, tools, or sources, which a single agent can use too.

The Anthropic example deserves credit for its honesty, but look at what it says. Anthropic reported that token usage alone explained roughly 80% of the performance variance. Its multi-agent system also used several times the tokens of a single agent. That is the compute confound, documented by the people who built the system. Anthropic also said the approach fits poorly with tightly coupled tasks like most coding.

So the defense has narrowed from "teams do better work" to "teams do better on broad, parallelizable research when cost is no object." I accept that narrower claim. Even there, the edge is eroding as context windows grow and single agents gain memory and compaction tools.

**My argument:** The topic is a general claim, and it fails as a general claim. The case for teams holds in a specific regime: tasks that split cleanly into independent pieces, have cheap external checks, and come with budgets large enough to absorb several times the cost. Most valuable work doesn't look like that. An essay, a product design, a legal argument, or a refactor of interdependent code all depend on one consistent vision. Splitting that vision across agents creates seams, conflicting implicit decisions, and an integrator working from summaries. A single capable agent with the same tools also has practical advantages. It is easier to debug, because there is one trace to read and no inter-agent miscommunication to untangle. Its errors are easier to attribute, and it costs far less. Teams are a useful technique for a particular class of problems, not a general recipe for better work. When resources are equal and the task needs coherence, one mind holding the whole problem usually does better.

I'm giving this one to the Against side. Both sides argued well and handled evidence honestly, but Against more consistently located the causal mechanism behind the For side's examples, and by the end For's position had narrowed to a regime that Against conceded without giving up the general claim.

output.reasoning: Both sides argued at a high level, handled evidence carefully, and each conceded fair points. Against wins on argument quality because it repeatedly identified the causal mechanism behind For's evidence and showed it was not teamwork itself. Self-consistency is repeated sampling. Grounded verification depends on the tool, not the teammate. Mixture-of-Agents and Anthropic's research system relied on extra inference, and Anthropic's own data showed token usage explained most of the performance variance. For answered some of this well. The point that a fresh-context verifier avoids inheriting the author's rationale was sharp, and so was the argument that parallelism lets teams turn compute into results on tasks too broad for one context window. But Against countered effectively: Huang et al., the paper For cited, found multi-agent debate no better than compute-matched self-consistency, and a fresh context resets the window, not the weights. For's final position, that teams win when tasks outgrow one mind, was a real but narrowed claim. Against explicitly accepted that narrow regime while arguing the general resolution fails for coherence-dependent work such as essays, design, and tightly coupled code. For never fully rebutted the 'equal conditions' framing, apart from the partial answer about serial context limits. As a result, Against left the debate with the more defensible account of the general claim.
